{{see also|History of group theory}}

The history of [[representation theory]] concerns the [[mathematics|mathematical]] development of the study of
objects in [[abstract algebra]], notably [[group (mathematics)|groups]], by describing these objects more concretely, particularly using [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] and [[linear algebra]]. In some ways, representation theory predates the mathematical objects it studies: for example, [[permutation group]]s (in [[algebra]]) and [[transformation group]]s (in [[geometry]]) were studied long before the notion of an abstract group was formalized by [[Arthur Cayley]] in 1854.<ref>{{Harvnb|Lam|1998}}.</ref><ref>{{Harvnb|Cayley|1854}}.</ref> Thus, in the [[history of algebra]], there was a process in which, first, mathematical objects were [[abstraction (mathematics)|abstracted]], and then the more abstract algebraic objects were realized or ''represented'' in terms of the more concrete ones, using [[homomorphism]]s, [[group action|actions]] and [[module (mathematics)|modules]].

An early pioneer of the [[representation theory of finite groups]] was [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Frobenius|1896}}, {{Harvnb|Frobenius|1897}}.</ref> At first this method was not widely appreciated, but with the development of [[character theory]] and the proof of [[Burnside's theorem|Burnside's <math>p^\alpha q^\beta</math> solvability criterion]] using such methods,<ref>{{Harvnb|Burnside|1904}}.</ref> its power was soon appreciated.<ref>In the first edition of his famous treatise, {{Harvnb|Burnside|1897}} writes "It may then be asked why... modes of representation, such as groups of linear transformations, are not even referred to. My answer
to this question is that while, in the present state of our knowledge, many results in the pure theory are arrived at most readily by dealing with properties of substitution groups, it would be difficult to find a result that
could be most directly obtained by the consideration of groups of linear transformations." In the second edition ({{Harvnb|Burnside|1911}}) he writes instead, "The theory of groups of linear substitutions has been the subject of numerous and important investigations by several writers; and the reason given in the original preface for omitting any account of it no longer holds good. In fact it is now more true to say that for further advances in the abstract theory one must look largely to the representation of group as a group of linear substitutions."</ref> Later [[Richard Brauer]] and others developed [[modular representation theory]].<ref>{{Harvb|Curtis|2003}}.</ref>
